Article Title: In 1981, Bea Gaddy began feeding neighbours in Baltimore on Thanksgiving; 45 years later, her daughter had only eight turkeys for thousands until chef Jose Andres and Maryland prison workers stepped i
Article Text:
Jose Andres and Maryland correctional services stepped in with food and other support (Facebook/Jose Andres)

Jose Andres offers support after appeal

Maryland correctional facility contributes hundreds of turkeys

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

How the Thanksgiving dinner began in 1981

With Thanksgiving approaching, Cynthia Brooks was facing the possibility of cancelling a food drive that has been part of Baltimore's community life for 45 years. The daughter of the late Bea Gaddy had only eight turkeys and limited supplies for an event meant to provide meals to people in need. Help arrived after celebrity chef Jose Andres and Maryland correctional services stepped in with food and other support, CBS News reported.The shortage was particularly difficult for Brooks because the annual dinner carries on work started by her mother in 1981. Gaddy had begun by preparing Thanksgiving meals at her home. Over the years, the effort grew into a community event, and Brooks took responsibility for continuing it. This year's preparations, however, were far from complete just days before the holiday.Brooks said donations had been slower than usual as families and businesses dealt with a difficult economic situation. The lack of supplies left her uncertain about whether she could organise the event at all. She appealed for public support, hoping that enough people and organisations would come forward to keep the tradition going.The response eventually came from several quarters. Andres offered help through his organisations, while the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services arranged a large turkey donation. The contributions helped address the shortage and allowed preparations for the Thanksgiving meal to move forward.The scale of the shortage became clear earlier in the week when Brooks spoke to WBAL-TV. The organisation had only 30 cans of string beans, 18 cans of corn and eight turkeys on Monday, despite having plans to provide meals to hundreds of people.According to the report, the original plan was to deliver food to as many as 500 people and host approximately 300 people for a sit-down Thanksgiving dinner. With so few supplies available, Brooks was struggling to see how the event could go ahead.The report caught the attention of Andres, who sharednthe coverage on social media and offered assistance. He said his organisations would work with the family services centre to make sure people received food.In his post on X, Andres wrote: "Tell them food will be in their way…we will contact them and help them and Longer Tables Fund will take care of it with the help of World Central Kitchen #BaltimoreStrong."The offer came through World Central Kitchen and the Longer Tables Fund. Brooks was surprised when she learnt about the sponsorship. Speaking to WBAL-TV, she reacted by saying, "What? I'm here screaming."She contacted the station again within an hour to confirm that the organisation had reached out to her. She was told that the entire meal would receive sponsorship, giving the organisers much-needed support at a critical stage of the preparations.World Central Kitchen was founded by Andres and works to provide meals during emergencies and crises. Its approach involves using available local resources and responding quickly to the food requirements of affected communities.The assistance was not limited to Andres' organisations. Maryland's Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services also contributed hundreds of turkeys for the Thanksgiving event.The birds were prepared by incarcerated individuals working at the Maryland Correctional Enterprises Meat Plant. The donation provided a substantial amount of the food needed for the event, which had been struggling to secure even basic supplies.Andres' team also agreed to prepare several dishes for the gathering. These included string beans, corn, sweet potatoes and stuffing. The contribution meant that the organisers would receive help with both the main food item and the accompanying dishes.Brooks said the support would make a significant difference to the meal. "They're preparing all the sides, the string beans, the corn, the sweet potatoes for the dinner, the stuffing for the dinner. It's going to be a great, great contribution to the meal," she told CBS News.For Brooks, the response also brought back the purpose behind her mother's work. She said the support reflected the willingness of people in Baltimore and Maryland to help others, even when the city faced its own difficulties."This city, with all of its faults and all of its things, it's a beautiful city. The spirit of our city is everything. It was that to her, and it's that to me," she said.She also spoke about her pride in the community's response. "It's makes me feel good. I'm so proud of the spirit of Baltimore, the spirit of Maryland. I'm so proud to be a Marylander," Brooks said.The annual meal traces its beginnings to Bea Gaddy, who started serving Thanksgiving food from her home in 1981. Her initiative eventually became a long-running community tradition, with her daughter continuing the work after her death.The Bea Gaddy Family Center now provides food, clothing and essential household items to individuals and families across the Greater Baltimore metropolitan area and other parts of Maryland.The centre's Thanksgiving programme is one part of this work. Its aim is to ensure that people who need assistance can access a holiday meal, whether through food deliveries or a community gathering.
Article Summary: Celebrity chef Jose Andres and Maryland correctional services stepped in with food and other support. Cynthia Brooks had only eight turkeys and limited supplies for an event meant to provide meals to people in need. She appealed for public support, hoping that enough people would come forward to keep the tradition going.

Article Title: A Maine collector founded an antique-car museum in 1963 and later created a trust to support it; 14 years after his death, trustees pledged $1 million to another museum, and the state's top court uphe
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How the collector established the museum and charitable trust

Why the $1 million donation became controversial

Why the Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld the gift

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A charitable trust established to preserve a collector's antique-car collection can also donate to another museum, provided it continues meeting its financial obligations and reasonably maintains the value of the trust as a whole. That principle was central to a dispute that reached Maine's highest court, after trustees pledged $1 million to a different automobile museum, prompting the original museum to challenge the donation.In a November 19, 2026, decision available on Justia, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld the trustees' decision, ruling that the donation did not violate the agreements governing the trust. The court found that the trustees had retained their discretion to manage the trust's assets, provided they continued supporting the original museum and reasonably maintained the value of the trust as a whole.The dispute dates back to collector Richard C Paine Jr., who established the Seal Cove Auto Museum in 1963 to maintain and display his extensive collection of antique automobiles. In 1986, he also established the Richard C Paine Jr. Automobile Collection Charitable Trust to support the collection and its preservation.After Paine died in 2007, the trust acquired most of his automobiles along with an endowment intended to support their maintenance and display.The trust and the museum had separate but closely connected responsibilities, with the trustees managing the trust's assets and the museum maintaining and exhibiting the collection.Over the years, disagreements between Seal Cove and the trustees resulted in substantial litigation. In an earlier 2020 decision, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court had recognised Seal Cove's status as a qualified beneficiary of the trust, allowing it to pursue claims concerning the trustees' management and conduct. The parties subsequently reached a settlement in 2020 and entered into an amended relationship agreement, effective January 1, 2021, to clarify their respective obligations.Under the amended agreement, the trust was required to provide Seal Cove with annual financial support of at least $200,000 or 4.5 per cent of its endowment assets, averaged over the previous 12 fiscal quarters, whichever amount was greater. The agreement also required the trustees to make investment decisions consistent with the goal of providing that support while reasonably protecting and maintaining the value of the trust's corpus, meaning its principal assets.In December 2021, trustee John J Sanford informed Seal Cove that the trust intended to donate $1 million from its endowment to the Owls Head Transportation Museum, another institution dedicated to transportation history and collections.The trust transferred the first $500,000 at the end of December 2021 and committed to paying the remaining $500,000 over five years. Seal Cove objected, arguing that the donation would reduce the endowment available to support its operations and therefore breach the agreements. In September 2022, it filed a motion seeking enforcement of the settlement, asking the court to direct the trustees to recover the money already transferred and cancel the remaining pledge.After a two-day evidentiary hearing, the Maine Business and Consumer Docket rejected Seal Cove's request in November 2025. The trial court found that the trust's overall value had increased since the agreements were made and that the donation had not undermined its long-term financial stability. Seal Cove appealed, arguing that the agreement's reference to the trust's corpus should be understood as referring specifically to its endowment fund, rather than all the trust's assets. It also challenged the trial court's decision to restrict the evidence presented during the hearing, contending that the trustees' broader conduct was relevant to the dispute.The Maine Supreme Judicial Court rejected both arguments. In its November 19 ruling, the court explained that the agreement clearly referred to the entire charitable trust when discussing the protection of its corpus. It noted that the agreement separately defined the term 'Endowment Assets', but did not use that term in the provision concerning the trust's corpus.The court also found that the trial court had appropriately limited the hearing to whether the Owls Head donation breached the settlement and amended relationship agreements. Other allegations concerning the trustees' conduct and their wider fiduciary responsibilities were outside the specific issue raised by the motion. Ultimately, the justices concluded that the evidence supported the finding that the trust's overall value remained protected and its annual financial obligations to Seal Cove continued to be met.The court found no breach of the settlement or amended relationship agreements and affirmed the lower court's judgment. This meant the trustees were not required to recover the $500,000 already donated or cancel the remaining $500,000 pledge.
Article Summary: A charitable trust established to preserve a collector's antique-car collection can also donate to another museum. That principle was central to a dispute that reached Maine's highest court. Trustees pledged $1 million to a different automobile museum, prompting the original museum to challenge the donation. The Maine Supreme Judicial Court upheld the trustees' decision.

A massive fire ripped through a commercial building on Thailand's southern resort island of Phuket early on Monday, killing at least 11 people and leaving 16 others injured, police told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the early hours of the morning and quickly spread to several nearby buildings, triggering a major firefighting operation.The fire erupted at around 3.17am local time (2017 GMT) at a shophouse housing a vehicle rental business. Firefighters battled the flames for nearly two hours before bringing the blaze under control, Thai authorities said.Of the 16 injured, 15 were Thai nationals while one was from Myanmar, police said. Article Title: GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play
Article Text:
GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play

Lander Allgood and Connor Folkers plan extended breaks for GTA 6 release

GTA flu: Why some gamers are planning to call in sick

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, November 19. Some have already booked their paid leave, while others are considering calling in sick to spend the day playing the long-awaited game. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the ‘GTA flu’ online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.For some players, the GTA 6 launch is worth planning their entire week around. Lander Allgood, a 26-year-old environmental specialist from the Dallas-Fort Worth area, requested two weeks of paid time off in July so he could enjoy the release.Allgood, who has played GTA 5 since he was around 13, compared the new game’s arrival to a major scientific achievement.“We’re basically witnessing, I mean, the Apollo space program of video games,” Allgood told USA TODAY.However, gaming is not his only responsibility. He plans to spend time with his two-year-old son and has arranged for his parents to look after the child from Thursday through Sunday. Once his son goes to bed, Allgood expects to spend hours playing.He is hoping to put in at least 20 hours over the weekend.Connor Folkers, a 22-year-old IT administrator from Iowa, has also arranged his schedule around the launch. He requested leave from November 19 through Thanksgiving and expects to spend more than 24 hours playing.For Folkers, getting enough time with the game before seeing other people’s reactions is important. He wants to experience the story and gameplay without online discussions shaping his opinion.“Really how I treat this game is sort of like a cultural event. You’re going to see this, I presume, everywhere online, whether it be story components or gameplay components, so I want to make sure I have enough time to really experience it for myself without the outside influencing my opinions on it,” Folkers told USA TODAY.He also compared the release to the Super Bowl, explaining how important the event has become for gaming enthusiasts.Not everyone is being upfront about taking a day off. Some players are planning to report sick on November 19 instead of requesting paid leave in advance.GameSquare surveyed 1,000 full-time US employees who identified as gamers. Its findings showed that 10% planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Among those considering leave, 36% said they would call in sick.BambooHR also found that nearly one in five salaried US workers planned to take time off for the release. Its figures showed that 32% of Gen Z employees and 27% of millennials intended to use paid leave to play.Nicole Csiszar, BambooHR’s director of HR, told USA TODAY that taking planned leave is a normal way for employees to enjoy their time away from work.“That’s a healthy sign,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “It means people are using PTO the way it’s meant to be used, to step away and do something they enjoy.”She also pointed out why some might choose to call in sick instead.“Requesting PTO in advance means submitting it, waiting on approval and sometimes explaining why you want the day,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “Calling in sick is one message that morning.”However, not every gamer is willing to put work aside. Ryan Van Dusen, a 42-year-old fifth-grade teacher from Michigan, has no plans to miss classes for the game. He is instead looking forward to playing during the Thanksgiving holiday.“My kids are expected to be in the classroom. I can’t take a day off from my students for this. This is preposterous,” Van Dusen told USA TODAY with a laugh. “In theory, Grand Theft Auto should be a small thing compared to work, family, things that are bigger. I think it’s healthy and good for us to have these small things that we can be excited for too and just to look forward to.”
Article Summary: Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the 'GTA flu' online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.

A fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season.Videos shared on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising near the stadium in East Rutherford and drifting over the playing field. One video also captured flames and black smoke erupting from the area near the venue.New Jersey State Police said troopers responded to a report of smoke shortly after 5:50 pm near Lot A and the stadium's American Express gate. They found a fire in an empty postgame tent, according to a report by Fox 5 New York.Fire crews brought the second-alarm blaze under control. No injuries or further damage were reported, while the cause of the fire was not immediately known.ESPN reporter Rich Cimini posted on social media that an announcement had been made inside the stadium about a “structure fire” near the adjacent train station. He later advised people to stay away from the stadium's east plaza, on the train station side, as smoke spread across the venue.Around 20 minutes later, he posted that the “situation has been resolved”.An NJ Transit spokesperson, quoted by NY Post said the fire did not disrupt train services in the area.The blaze broke out hours after the Jets lost 31-12 to the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium. The defeat marked their fifth straight loss, leaving them with a 2-8 record for the season.The Jets struggled against the Bills, who secured a 19-point victory. The loss extended New York's losing streak and added to a difficult season for the team.
Article Summary: Fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday. The blaze sent thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season. No injuries or further damage were reported. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Article Title: 'He is my friend': Trump, Putin hold talks ahead of trilateral meeting with Xi on APEC sidelines
Article Text:
Trump Putin hold talks ahead of trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping

Trump-Putin meeting ahead of trilateral talks

Xi and Putin reaffirm strategic partnership

Putin criticises economic restrictions, calls for fairer world order

Nuclear arms control and Iran on trilateral agenda

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump held bilateral talks with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, ahead of a trilateral discussion with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.The meeting was held on the sidelines of APEC summit in Chinese city of Shenzhen.Trump expressed optimism ahead of the meeting"A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start", he said."We will have a second meeting later on," he added.The meeting comes amid heightened diplomatic activity involving Washington, Moscow and Beijing, with the three leaders expected to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war and global trade. The proposed trilateral engagement is being closely watched as a possible opportunity to address some of the most pressing geopolitical challenges.Trump arrived at the APEC venue earlier in the day, where he was welcomed by Xi. The US president subsequently met Putin, with the two leaders exchanging handshakes before joining other world leaders for a group photograph.The bilateral engagement between Trump and Putin comes a day after the Russian president held extensive discussions with Xi, reaffirming the strength of Moscow's strategic partnership with Beijing.The Trump-Putin meeting assumes importance as Washington and Moscow seek to address differences over the Ukraine war and the future of nuclear arms control.Trump had indicated before departing for Asia that the proposed discussions with Putin and Xi would cover several major international issues, including nuclear disarmament, Iran, Ukraine and economic relations."We're going to be talking about denuclearisation...We'll talk about Iran," Trump told reporters ahead of his departure.He also identified the Russia-Ukraine war as a key subject of discussion."We'll also talk about my favourite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine is losing. Ukraine and Russia are losing 25,000 souls per month, so we'll be talking about that. We'll also discuss economics and trade," Trump said.The proposed trilateral meeting would bring together the leaders of three major powers at a time when diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict have faced challenges.The prospect of discussions involving Washington and Moscow without Ukraine's direct participation has also raised concerns in Kyiv and among its European partners.Ahead of Trump's arrival, Xi and Putin held bilateral discussions in Shenzhen on Wednesday, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening economic, political and strategic cooperation.Xi described the relationship between China and Russia as resilient amid international uncertainty, saying their ties "stand as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain".He called on both countries to adopt a long-term strategic approach and shoulder greater responsibilities as major powers in shaping the international order."We must firmly shoulder the responsibilities expected of major powers, lead and advance the multipolarisation of the world and the democratisation of international relations," Xi said.Putin, meanwhile, described political cooperation between Moscow and Beijing as constructive despite the challenging international environment."Russian-Chinese political cooperation is working favourably and constructively in a difficult political situation," Putin stated."We are committed to constructive approaches to form a fairer multipolar world order," he added.The two leaders also discussed the need to expand cooperation across sectors, with Xi describing their partnership as a model of equality, mutual respect and mutually beneficial cooperation.According to Russian media reports, the discussions continued over a working breakfast in Shenzhen on Wednesday.Putin also addressed business representatives at the APEC CEO Summit, where he criticised the use of tariffs, sanctions and export restrictions as instruments of geopolitical and economic pressure.He argued that countries were increasingly seeking greater economic sovereignty and independence amid changes in the global geopolitical landscape."The regional model serves as a vivid example of strengthening a fairer, more democratic and equal world order," Putin said, referring to developments in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president criticised attempts by established economic powers to restrict the growth of emerging economies, arguing that such measures undermined fair competition and could ultimately hurt the countries imposing them.Putin acknowledged that tariffs, export restrictions and sanctions continued to affect economic development."But they are not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying the economies of the competition," he added.He also expressed expectations of "great use" from the proposed trilateral meeting involving Trump, Xi and himself.The proposed meeting comes at a sensitive moment for international nuclear arms control following the expiration of the New START treaty between the United States and Russia in February 2026.Trump has expressed interest in negotiating a new nuclear arms control framework that would include China alongside Washington and Moscow.However, Beijing has traditionally resisted joining such negotiations, pointing to the considerably larger nuclear arsenals maintained by the United States and Russia.The Iran conflict is another issue expected to feature in the discussions, alongside disagreements over international trade, tariffs, technology restrictions and global supply chains.China has described the proposed trilateral engagement as being of "ground-breaking significance", with the potential to safeguard global peace and promote strategic stability among major powers.The APEC summit has consequently emerged as an important diplomatic platform for Washington, Moscow and Beijing to engage on issues ranging from nuclear security to regional conflicts and the future of the global economic order.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump held bilateral talks with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, ahead of a trilateral discussion with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The meeting was held on the sidelines of APEC summit in Chinese city of Shenzhen. The proposed trilateral engagement is being closely watched as a possible opportunity to address some of the most pressing geopolitical challenges.

Article Title: ‘US invented superintelligence’: Trump flags AI dangers but rejects global regulation at Apec summit
Article Text:
Donald Trump spoke at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting

US president Donald Trump on Thursday opposed international efforts to regulate or restrict the development of superintelligence (SI), saying Washington would not allow measures that could stifle the technology.Addressing the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, he described SI as the biggest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution.“The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, SI, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution. It's amazing when you say that, but it seems to be true. Americans invented—we just invented SI, and it is unleashing extraordinary prosperity and growth for people all around the globe,” Trump said.While promoting the technology’s potential, Trump acknowledged that its development could carry risks and called for safeguards to manage them.“We have to watch it. We have to be careful. We have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements,” he said.However, he ruled out global regulatory measures, arguing that they could impede innovation.“So we oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle SI, and we won't allow that to happen, frankly,” Trump added.Trump also used the address to highlight his administration’s economic record, claiming that inflation had remained below two per cent over the preceding three months.“The last 3 months, inflation was down to a number that was not expected. We were able to do a real job. You know, a lot of other countries are having difficulty with that, but we've gotten it less than 2% for the last 3 months,” he said.He claimed the US had secured commitments worth $22.2 trillion in new investments and generated $25 trillion in new wealth up to November 1. Trump also said investment in new equipment had risen by 21 per cent this year and exports had reached a record high.He attributed the claimed gains to tax cuts, deregulation and trade agreements, saying the administration had concluded more than 20 deals. He also indicated that further agreements with major economies were being negotiated.Trump promoted US energy exports, referring to an approved liquefied natural gas pipeline project in Alaska intended to supply Asian markets. He also said American oil companies were “moving in” to Venezuela, adding: “We’re doing tremendous business in Venezuela.”His comments on SI come days after the US and nine partner countries, including India, signed the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity on November 15. Signed at the Pax Silica Founders Retreat, the declaration seeks cooperation on sensitive technologies, critical infrastructure and supply-chain security.The signatories also include Australia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.The declaration sets out a framework for trusted supply chains and international cooperation as emerging technologies develop.
Article Summary: Donald Trump spoke at the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China. He described SI as the biggest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution. Trump acknowledged that its development could carry risks and called for safeguards.

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: Washington governor Bob Ferguson says ICE is 'out of control' & 'deeply un-American' after airport arrest

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson has accused US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) of using "deeply un-American" tactics after federal agents detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle, triggering a confrontation with passengers boarding a flight to Los Angeles.Ferguson criticised the operation at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, alleging that masked officers had created chaos by removing passengers during the boarding process. He said the incident raised concerns about how federal immigration enforcement was being conducted in public spaces."ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson wrote on X. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."The arrests took place at around 8.05am local time on Alaska Airlines Flight 1306's jet bridge, shortly before the aircraft was scheduled to depart for Los Angeles. ICE said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who allegedly remained in the United States after his visa expired.Federal agents also detained another passenger, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia. According to ICE, she had also overstayed her visa and threw hot coffee at officers during the operation.The agency said she could face charges of assaulting a federal officer and warned that anyone interfering with law enforcement would face prosecution.Footage of the incident circulating online showed masked officers pulling people away from the boarding area as other passengers watched. A woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being detained and had a work permit. Officers were also seen struggling with an individual on the floor.The airport operation also drew criticism from Alaska Airlines, which said it had received no advance notification of the enforcement action. The airline expressed concern about the arrests taking place while passengers were boarding its aircraft."We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said in a statement.It added that the incident had caused distress among passengers and employees and that it was working with the Port of Seattle to determine whether established procedures had been followed. The airline said it had raised its concerns directly with the relevant authorities.
Article Summary: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle. The arrests triggered a confrontation with passengers boarding a flight to Los Angeles. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson accused ICE of using "deeply un-American" tactics.

Article Title: A judge has let a lawsuit against Delta go ahead from passengers who say they paid extra for a window seat only to find a blank wall, after one flyer’s seat 23F on a Boeing 757 had no window at all
Article Text:
Why Delta wanted the case dismissed

United Airlines is facing a similar lawsuit

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Passengers who paid extra to secure window seats on Delta Air Lines flights may have expected an outside view, but some say they ended up staring at a blank cabin wall instead. A federal judge in New York has now allowed a proposed class-action lawsuit against the airline to proceed, rejecting Delta’s attempt to have the case dismissed. The November 4, 2026 ruling, reported by Reuters, Law360 and Insurance Journal, keeps alive claims that Delta charged passengers for window seats without clearly disclosing that some of those seats had no actual windows. However, the decision does not establish that the airline broke the law. The allegations will now have to be examined as the case moves forward.The dispute began with Nicholas Meyer, who booked a journey from New York’s LaGuardia Airport to Orange County, California, on August 16, 2025, with a stop in Atlanta. According to the lawsuit, he paid extra to select window seats on both flights because he wanted to look outside during the journey. His first seat, 32A, had a window. The second leg was a different experience. After boarding a Boeing 757-200 in Atlanta, Meyer discovered that his assigned seat, 23F, was positioned beside a blank section of the aircraft wall.He argued that he would not have selected or paid extra for the seat had Delta disclosed that it did not have a window.The lawsuit was initially filed in August 2025, with three additional passengers, Anthony Bernardo, Justin Valentine and Leah Roberts, joining it in October that year. Meyer subsequently withdrew his individual claims in May 2026, leaving the other three passengers to continue the case.Delta challenged the lawsuit by arguing that its Conditions of Carriage do not guarantee passengers particular seat assignments. The airline also maintained that it needs the flexibility to change aircraft and seating arrangements depending on operational requirements. Another part of its defence relied on the federal Airline Deregulation Act, which limits certain state-level regulation of airline services and pricing. Delta argued that the passengers’ claims were barred under the law.However, US District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr., sitting in Brooklyn, rejected the airline’s request to dismiss the case on November 4. The court found that there was a legitimate question over whether Delta’s contractual terms required it to provide the window seats passengers believed they had purchased. It also allowed the claims to proceed despite Delta’s argument about federal law.Delta is not the only airline dealing with allegations over windowless window seats. United Airlines is facing a separate proposed class-action lawsuit brought by passengers who say they paid additional fees for seats advertised as window seats but discovered there was no window beside them.In July 2026, US District Judge James Donato in San Francisco also rejected United’s attempt to dismiss the case. The judge pointed to the airline’s booking screens and boarding passes, which identified the selected seats as window seats, allowing the passengers’ contractual claims to move forward.The issue stems partly from aircraft design. On some planes, structural components such as air-conditioning ducts and electrical systems occupy spaces behind the cabin walls where windows would ordinarily be installed. This can leave certain seats without an outside view, even though they are positioned along the aircraft’s exterior wall.For passengers, the distinction is significant because window seats are often chosen for more than their position in the cabin. Some travellers prefer them to avoid being disturbed by people moving through the aisle, while others choose them for the view, natural light or simply the comfort of having a wall beside them.The Delta and United cases could therefore have implications for how airlines describe seats during the booking process, particularly when passengers are charged extra for selecting them. For now, neither lawsuit has resulted in a finding of wrongdoing or a compensation award. The courts have only allowed the claims to proceed, leaving the central question unanswered: When an airline sells a window seat, should passengers be able to expect an actual window?
Article Summary: Passengers who paid extra to secure window seats on Delta Air Lines flights may have expected an outside view, but some say they ended up staring at a blank cabin wall instead. A federal judge in New York has now allowed a proposed class-action lawsuit against the airline to proceed. The November 4, 2026 ruling keeps alive claims that Delta charged passengers for window seats without clearly disclosing that some of those seats had no actual windows.

Article Title: In 2022, a New York family partnership bought Galloo Island for $5.8 million; a $3 million conservation easement now protects 1,410 acres on Lake Ontario without transferring ownership or opening the
Article Text:
A $3 million deal to protect the island

Ownership remains with the Patten family

Why Galloo Island matters to conservationists

A significant addition to New York’s conservation efforts

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A privately owned island in Lake Ontario has received permanent conservation protection after a major agreement with a New York land trust. The Thousand Islands Land Trust (TILT) has secured a conservation easement covering 1,410 acres of Galloo Island, protecting its forests, wetlands, shoreline and wildlife habitats from future development. The agreement, reported by local broadcaster WWNY and The Land Report, is the largest conservation project by acreage in TILT’s history. The organisation announced the protection as a significant step towards safeguarding one of the region’s ecologically important landscapes.The conservation agreement was completed in partnership with Galloo Island Farms, the family partnership that acquired the property in December 2021 for $5.8 million. The purchase was made by the Patten family, which had previously owned much of the island and returned with plans to restore its farmland and protect its natural landscape.According to The Land Report, the conservation easement is valued at approximately $3.1 million, while WWNY reported the expenditure at $3 million. It is the largest single conservation expenditure made by the Thousand Islands Land Trust. The easement covers roughly 70 per cent of Galloo Island, making it a substantial addition to the region’s protected land.The agreement was negotiated between TILT, Galloo Island Farms and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.Despite the conservation agreement, Galloo Island has not become public property. The Patten family retains ownership of the protected land, and the easement does not amount to a sale or transfer of the island to the land trust. Instead, it is a legally binding arrangement that places restrictions on how the property can be used and developed. These conditions are intended to ensure that the island’s natural features remain protected even if ownership changes in the future.The agreement also does not make Galloo Island a new tourist destination. Visitors cannot assume they have public access to the property, and restrictions extend to activities around the shoreline, including fishing. The arrangement is an example of how conservation easements allow private landowners to retain their property while permanently limiting activities that could damage its environmental value.Located in Lake Ontario, Galloo Island is recognised for its diverse natural habitats, including forests, wetlands, grasslands and extensive shoreline. These environments provide shelter and feeding grounds for a range of wildlife, including rare, threatened and endangered species.The island also serves as an important stopover for migratory birds and monarch butterflies. Among the wildlife recorded in the area are short-eared owls and golden eagles. For TILT, protecting the island is particularly significant because of its ecological importance and the development pressures it has faced over the years. Earlier proposals for wind energy projects had raised concerns about the island’s future, although neither project ultimately moved forward. The latest conservation agreement provides long-term protection for the landscape while allowing the property to remain privately owned.Founded in 1984, the Thousand Islands Land Trust works to protect natural landscapes, wildlife habitats, water quality and outdoor recreation opportunities across the Thousand Islands region, which stretches along the US-Canada border. According to its website, the organisation has protected more than 15,000 acres through land ownership and conservation easements. Its portfolio includes forests, wetlands, shoreline properties and nature preserves.The Galloo Island agreement adds to those efforts and marks TILT’s first conservation easement purchase in the eastern part of Lake Ontario. While the island will remain privately owned and unavailable for general public recreation, its forests, wetlands and wildlife habitats now have an additional layer of permanent legal protection. The agreement ensures that the island’s ecological value will be considered in how the land is managed for generations to come.
Article Summary: The Thousand Islands Land Trust has secured a conservation easement covering 1,410 acres of Galloo Island. The agreement is the largest conservation project by acreage in TILT’s history. The Patten family acquired the property in December 2021 for $5.8 million. The easement does not amount to a sale or transfer of the island to the land trust.

Article Title: Companies diverted Trump's $100bn tariff refunds to bonuses, not consumers: Report
Article Text:
Trump administration has refunded at least $100 billion to companies since August, accounting for about 60 per cent of the roughly $165 billion collected in tariffs.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Several companies that received refunds for tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump have directed some of the money towards corporate bonuses rather than reimbursing consumers, according to a report.After examining securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies that disclosed receiving tariff refunds and indicated that some of the money would go towards compensation for their leadership, The Guardian reported.Toolmaker Stanley Black & Decker, which makes products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, had told consumers that it was forced to raise prices because of Trump's import fees. The company is expected to receive at least $298 million in tariff refunds and indicated that part of the amount would go towards bonuses, according to ProPublica.Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, both owned by parent company TJX, also indicated that tariff refunds would contribute to employee bonuses. A TJX spokesperson confirmed that the company had received a total of $331 million in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered by the Supreme Court ruling.The spokesperson said the refunds had resulted in “incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”. The company added that it had not disclosed a further breakdown because the amount was still an accrual and its current financial year had not ended.In its financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, ProPublica reported. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The Trump administration has refunded at least $100 billion to companies since August, accounting for about 60 per cent of the roughly $165 billion collected in tariffs. The refunds followed a Supreme Court ruling that Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs were unlawful because they exceeded his executive authority and required congressional approval.Some companies immediately sued the US government seeking refunds after the ruling. Trump, however, said he would “remember” which companies sought reimbursements and praised those that held off. The administration has not disclosed which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.While several companies had said they increased prices because of tariffs, it has largely remained unclear how they intend to use the reimbursements. ProPublica found that most companies publicly committing to refund customers were those dealing directly with other businesses rather than consumers. Others have remained vague about whether they would use the money to lower prices or avoid future increases.Research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimated that 26 per cent of tariff increases are passed on to consumer prices, while the Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost US households around $900 annually under current laws.
Article Summary: Several companies that received refunds for tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump have directed some of the money towards corporate bonuses. Trump administration has refunded at least $100 billion to companies since August, accounting for about 60 per cent of the roughly $165 billion collected in tariffs.

Article Title: A 61-year-old Pennsylvania supermarket employee bought a scratch-off ticket on her lunch break, and when it lost, she bought another, which won $1 million; she plans to keep working at the store where
Article Text:
A ‘lucky’ lunch break

She plans to continue working

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sometimes, all it takes is one more try for luck to find you. And that's exactly what 61-year-old Andrea Rothwell did. She was on her lunch break when she bought a scratch-off ticket at Tops Friendly Markets in Youngsville, Pennsylvania, where she has worked for five years. Her first scratch-off was a loser, and she turned to leave. But then something told her she had to give it another try. So she went back, and the second ticket she bought won $1 million. It’s no surprise that her co-workers, family, friends and even acquaintances think she has luck on her side. But that’s not the whole story. She did something most people don’t. She gave it a second try. And, well, luck decided to be her pal."So many times, you hear about people winning on the next ticket. I'm glad I went back," she said in a statement to the Pennsylvania Lottery.Despite winning a fortune, Rothwell plans to continue working at the store.Andrea Rothwell, 61, from Warren County, works as the dairy and frozen foods manager at Tops Friendly Markets in Youngsville, Pennsylvania. "I was on my lunch break," Rothwell recalls. During her break, she stopped at the machine and decided to buy a ticket."I actually bought that same ticket twice. The first ticket was a loser. So, I walked away from the machine but then decided to try one more time. That ticket turned out to be the big winner!" She won $1 million from the Million Dollar Win It All ticket, which she bought for $50. That’s not the kind of money she expected to win. So, Rothwell did not trust what she saw at first. She had to ask a co-worker to check the ticket and confirm the number of zeros!Winning a million dollars does not mean Rothwell is retiring. She plans to continue working at the store, where she has been employed for five years. So, what is she going to do with her winnings? She plans to invest the money and help her family.Andrea Rothwell’s colleagues are thrilled by her win. "We couldn't be happier for Andrea," Jay Knavel, district manager for Tops Friendly Markets, said in a statement. "Andrea has been part of our Youngsville Tops family for five years, and sharing in her excitement makes this celebration especially meaningful. Her plans to help her family speak to what matters most to her, and our entire team is thrilled to celebrate this incredible moment with her. "The Pennsylvania Lottery and Tops Friendly Markets hosted a commemorative cheque presentation on Thursday, 19 November, at the supermarket at 28 Railroad Avenue in Youngsville Borough to celebrate the lucky winner."Celebrating our winners is what it's all about. We are happy that Andrea took a chance on the Lottery during her lunch break and won," Pennsylvania Lottery Executive Director Drew Svitko said. "Our retailers, including Tops Friendly Markets, also play an incredibly important role in serving our players and supporting the Lottery's mission of benefiting older Pennsylvanians."Meanwhile, Tops Friendly Markets will also receive a $5,000 bonus for selling the winning ticket. Scratch-off tickets are distributed at random. The Lottery and its retailers do not know where a winning ticket will be sold until a prize is claimed.Pennsylvania is the only state that directs all its lottery proceeds to programmes for older residents, according to the Lottery. Since ticket sales began in 1972, the state says it has contributed more than $38.2 billion to services such as transport, care services, prescription assistance, senior centres and meals."Our team at the Department of Revenue congratulates Andrea on her $1 million prize, and we wish her all the best as she plans for the future. Her win is a reminder that it only takes one ticket to win a life-changing prize," Secretary of Revenue Pat Browne said. "It's also important to remember that every Pennsylvania Lottery ticket helps support programmes and services for older Pennsylvanians. Since its inception close to 55 years ago, the Pennsylvania Lottery has contributed billions of dollars to programmes that benefit older adults in communities across the Commonwealth. "
Article Summary: Andrea Rothwell, 61, from Warren County, works as the dairy and frozen foods manager at Tops Friendly Markets in Youngsville, Pennsylvania. She won $1 million from the Million Dollar Win It All ticket, which she bought for $50. Despite winning a fortune, Rothwell plans to continue working at the store.

Article Title: US immigration authorities detain Indian-origin man after Texas criminal conviction
Article Text:
In Texas, Raghul Anandakrishnan, a 29-year-old of Indian descent, has been apprehended by immigration officials following his conviction for attempting invasive visual recording.

US immigration authorities in Texas have arrested a 29-year-old Indian-origin man following his conviction for attempted invasive visual recording. Officials said he will remain in federal detention until the immigration court completes its proceedings.The US immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) took custody of Raghul Anandakrishnan from a county jail in Texas, the agency said in a post on Sunday.According to ICE, Anandakrishnan had served time in the county jail following his conviction in a case involving the unauthorised transfer of explicit photographs from a woman's mobile phone.The case came to light after a woman alleged that an employee at a wireless phone store had accessed her device and transferred her intimate pictures without her consent, according to news agency PTI.In its post on X, ICE said, "ICE took custody of him from the county jail. He'll remain in ICE custody pending immigration court proceedings."The detention follows a criminal case registered in Austin in June. Records from the Austin police department and Travis County court filings, cited by local media, showed that Anandakrishnan was arrested while working at a Total Wireless store.According to court affidavits, he allegedly transferred two intimate photographs from a customer's phone to his own device using Apple's airdrop feature.He also allegedly accessed the customer's Snapchat account.Travis County jail records showed that he was initially booked on June 7 on charges of invasive visual recording and computer security breach. His bond was set at a combined USD 10,000, and no-contact orders were imposed.He was subsequently convicted of attempted invasive visual recording.Federal authorities have not yet disclosed further details about his immigration status, the facility where he is currently being held or the dates of his upcoming immigration court proceedings.

Officials said he will remain in federal detention until the immigration court completes its proceedings. The detention follows a criminal case registered in Austin in June. He was convicted of attempted invasive visual recording.

Article Title: Chicago artist Mary Ellen Croteau collected more than 7,000 bottle caps over two years; she turned them into an 8-by-7-foot self-portrait
Article Text:
Chicago artist Mary Ellen Croteau and CLOSE, a self-portrait built from bottle caps. Image Credits: Mary Ellen Croteau/Facebook

CLOSE

Two years of collecting, seven months of building

CLOSE

Melting Glacier, Greenland, one of Croteau's later bottle-cap pictures of ecological disasters. Image Credits: Mary Ellen Croteau/Facebook

Why plastic became her material

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More than one portrait

CLOSE

CLOSE

My Eye

Wildfire

Alberta 2015

Melting Glacier, Greenland

Tsunami

Most plastic bottle caps disappear into a bin and are forgotten within seconds. Mary Ellen Croteau, a Chicago-based artist who passed away in 2019, gave thousands of them new lives. The Mary Ellen Croteau website shares that she collected more than 7,000 bottle caps over two years. She spent seven months turning them into, an 8-foot by 7-foot self-portrait. The work is colourful and impossible to ignore. It also raises a simple question: where does plastic waste actually end up?is a huge self-portrait that used more than 7,000 plastic bottle caps. Collecting this many caps took two years, which amounts to an average of 10 plastic caps daily. Creating the portrait took another seven months. According to her website, this artwork is dated as far back as 2011. It lists the size as 8 feet by 7 feet, or about 2.4 by 2.1 metres. That work is part of her bottle caps series that ran from 2010 to 2019. The caps were not collected from just one source. Her material included plastic waste that her friends and family collected in their own homes. She also used plastic garbage that she got from dumpsters at a recycling centre at North Park Village.Her goal was to bring attention to the litter that was often left unrecycled.Croteau’s website explains her idea in simple words. Plastic does not compost or biodegrade and is made from petroleum. What little gets recycled can also end up causing pollution in its own way. She said that single-serve plastic bottles are the worst kind of plastic and excessive packaging comes next. The site adds that her aim was to make this waste visible and to connect throwaway culture with responsibility for the Earth.Research shows the extent of the problem. The 2017 Science Advances study by Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law estimated that some 6.3 billion metric tons of plastic waste had been produced by 2015. About 9% of it was recycled, 12% incinerated, and 79% ended up in landfills or the natural environment. The same paper found that some 42% of all non-fibre plastics produced had been used to make packaging. The same pattern was seen in the United States as well, where Croteau lived.Data from the Environmental Protection Agency for 2018 showed that the nation produced 35.7 million American tons of plastic. This made up 12.2% of its municipal solid waste. Only three million tons were recycled. That was 8.7% of the plastic produced. PET bottles and jars fared better at a recycling rate of 29.1%, but still, the majority of them were not recycled.was part of a larger body of work. Plastic World, a spring 2013 exhibition, ran from 1 April to 5 May at the Northwestern University’s Dittmar Memorial Gallery. It included nine of Croteau’s works, including. Other works included A Measure of Consumption, a 175-foot installation of about 600 plastic bags. Another,, was a close-up of her own eye made from bottle caps and lids of different sizes. Croteau's later work in the series shifted to larger themes. She described them as large pictures of ecological disasters made out of bottle caps. Titles includeand. There is also a how-to guide on the website for anyone who wants to give bottle cap art a shot. One artwork might not solve the problem of plastic around the world, but it can make the problem a lot easier to see.
Article Summary: Chicago-based artist Mary Ellen Croteau collected more than 7,000 bottle caps over two years. She spent seven months turning them into, an 8-foot by 7-foot self-portrait. The work is part of her bottle caps series that ran from 2010 to 2019.

Article Title: A homeless Marine veteran in Colorado Springs received an unexpected gift from local support groups: a donated car he says will help him reach medical appointments and search for an apartment as he re
Article Text:
Jones can now travel for medical care and explore housing options (AI image)

When Jones lost his car

How the community arranged the car

What the car means for Jones and his dog

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A donated car has given a 68-year-old Marine Corps veteran in Colorado Springs a chance to regain some independence after months of homelessness and health difficulties. Thurman “Hank” Jones Jr. received a car from Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center and medical transport company MedRide on Thursday. He hopes to use it to attend medical appointments, find affordable accommodation and look for employment.Jones had been without a vehicle after the one he previously owned broke down. The loss made an already difficult situation harder, as he was also dealing with cancer and had been living without a permanent home. His new car came through efforts by people who learnt about his circumstances and decided to help him.The donation was made possible through cooperation between local organisations. KRDO reported that several groups had spent weeks arranging the vehicle for Jones. According to The Gazette, the effort began after Bob McLaughlin, executive director of Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center, learnt that the veteran needed transport.For Jones, the gift addresses a practical problem that had affected several parts of his daily life. He can now travel for medical care and explore housing options instead of having to manage these journeys on foot. He also hopes the vehicle will help him and his dog, Dottie, as they try to move towards a more stable situation.Jones' housing problems began about eight months before the car was donated. He was evicted from his residence and subsequently stayed in his vehicle with Dottie.That arrangement did not last. When the car stopped working, Jones had to sell it. A city ordinance prohibited people from living in their vehicles, a practice known as vehicle camping. Losing the car therefore left him without both a place to stay and a means of getting around.Travelling through Colorado Springs was particularly difficult without personal transport. The city has hilly terrain, making it harder for Jones to cover distances on foot. He spoke about the difficulty of navigating the area at his age.“There’s nothing flat in this town,” Jones told The Gazette, explaining that getting around on foot had become difficult.His health concerns added to the challenges. The veteran had been dealing with cancer and needed a reliable way to reach medical appointments. Without a vehicle, even routine travel had become a concern.Jones also wanted to find another place to live. Having transport would allow him to visit apartments, compare what he could afford and take steps towards leaving homelessness behind.The effort to find a vehicle began after Jones spoke to McLaughlin about the problems he was facing. The Mt. Carmel executive director knew the veteran and understood that the absence of transport was affecting his ability to manage everyday needs.McLaughlin decided to approach people in the community to see whether someone could help. His search led to a meeting with Tyler Borzileri of MedRide in Pueblo about three weeks before the car was handed over.During their conversation, McLaughlin mentioned that a veteran needed a vehicle. Borzileri said the medical transport company had one it could donate.The organisation then prepared the car before transferring it to Jones. MedRide technicians removed the company's branding from the sedan, cleaned it inside and outside, and carried out a tune-up. The vehicle had previously been used for the company's transport operations.Borzileri assured Jones that the car had been refurbished and was in good condition before handing him the keys.The presentation took place at Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center on November 19. Jones appeared overwhelmed when he saw the vehicle and was initially unable to say much about the gesture.The new car is expected to make it easier for Jones to attend medical appointments, travel around Colorado Springs and look for work. It will also give him the flexibility to visit potential apartments and assess housing options.After receiving the keys, Jones said he planned to visit the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) first to complete the necessary formalities to make the vehicle road legal. He also intended to meet a close friend who had supported him during difficult periods.Dottie, his dog, will also benefit from having a way to travel with him. The two had been living together in his car after he lost his residence, before the vehicle broke down.Jones said the support had affected him emotionally as well as practically. His circumstances had sometimes made him feel that he was not worthy of receiving help. The donation changed that feeling.He described the gesture as something that had made him feel valued during a difficult period. He also expressed gratitude towards the people and organisations that had stepped in to help.Jones said he had lived in different parts of the country but had not experienced the same kind of community support he found in Colorado Springs. He particularly appreciated the people at Mt. Carmel Veterans Service Center.The donated car does not resolve all the difficulties Jones faces, including his housing and health concerns. However, it gives him a way to deal with some immediate challenges and pursue the next steps towards greater independence.
Article Summary: Thurman ‘Hank’ Jones Jr. lost his car after it broke down. The 68-year-old had been living in his car for eight months. He was evicted and had to sell the car, leaving him homeless. He also had health problems and needed a reliable way to get to medical appointments.

Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

Article Title: 4.0-magnitude earthquake strikes Pakistan near Afghanistan border
Article Text:
Image source: NCS

This is a breaking copy, further information is awaited.

A 4.0-magnitude earthquake struck Pakistan on Sunday morning, with tremors recorded in the region, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS).The earthquake occurred at 9.18am IST at a depth of 13km, with its epicentre at latitude 32.794°N and longitude 69.745°E. The event was marked as “reviewed” by the NCS.The epicentre was located 202km south-southeast of Kabul, Afghanistan, and 322km west-southwest of Islamabad.
