Article Title: $135 billion in debt, still getting loans: Who is keeping Pakistan afloat, and why
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and chief of defence forces Asim Munir (Reuters file photo)

What World Bank’s International Debt Report says about Pakistan

Pakistan’s economic challenges

China: Pakistan’s ‘all-weather’ friend

Why financial institutions continue lending to Pakistan

Can Pakistan actually repay its debt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens if creditors stop lending to Pakistan

The World Bank ’s International Debt Report 2026 paints a stark picture of Pakistan’s growing external debt burden, showing that, as of 2025, Islamabad’s external debt had nearly doubled from its 2015 level.According to the report, Pakistan’s external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015, marking a 97% increase in just 10 years.Pakistan's mounting external debt presents a curious contradiction. Its economy continues to struggle, and its dependence on foreign financing remains substantial. Yet, despite these vulnerabilities, money continues to flow into the country from some of the world's most influential governments and financial institutions.The question, therefore, is not simply why Islamabad keeps borrowing, but why its creditors continue lending to a country whose ability to generate sufficient foreign exchange and meet its repayment obligations remains a source of concern.The $135.1 billion, which Pakistan owed as external debt, was up 4% from $129.9 billion in 2024. Of the 2025 debt, around $107.1 billion was public and publicly guaranteed debt, while the remainder included private-sector and short-term external obligations.Of Pakistan’s public and publicly guaranteed debt, nearly $57 billion is owed to multilateral creditors, while bilateral creditors account for over $42 billion, with the remainder owed to private creditors.Among individual creditors, China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. It is followed by the World Bank, with $19.2 billion, and the Asian Development Bank, with $16.83 billion, among other creditors.The report also highlighted the burden of debt repayments on Pakistan’s economy. In 2025, Islamabad spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt, while total external debt stood at 34% of Gross National Income.The report, therefore, highlights the challenge facing Islamabad: managing its growing external debt while ensuring that its economy generates enough foreign exchange to meet repayment obligations.Continued lending does not necessarily mean Pakistan’s economy is healthy. Nor does its growing debt burden mean the country is on the verge of default.The latest economic indicators present a mixed picture.The World Bank estimates that Pakistan’s economy grew by 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% in the previous financial year. The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP, while the current account recorded a small deficit of 0.1% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also reported that Pakistan’s gross foreign exchange reserves had risen to approximately $21.5 billion by the end of September 2025.These gains, however, are offset by continued economic challenges. Economic growth has not generated enough jobs for Pakistan’s growing workforce. About 3.5 million people enter the workforce every year, yet unemployment stood at 7% in 2024. While nearly 18 million new jobs have been created since 2018, most have been informal, low-paid or self-employment opportunities.Poverty, too, has increased, with the rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. An estimated 70 million Pakistanis are now living in poverty.The future outlook also remains challenging. The World Bank projected Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.8% in FY27, a marginal increase from the estimated 3.7% growth in FY26. Headline inflation was expected to rise to 8.2% in FY27 before easing to around 7%.The data therefore highlights the economic pressures Pakistan faces and is expected to confront in the coming years.China being Pakistan’s largest individual creditor is perhaps unsurprising. Beijing and Islamabad are, after all, each other’s “all-weather friends.”China’s investment in Pakistan has largely been channelled through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the flagship project of Beijing’s ambitious Belt and Road Initiative. Under CPEC, Chinese investment in Pakistan is estimated at $62 billion over a period of 15 years.Another important feature of this economic relationship is loan rollover, under which a creditor extends the repayment period of existing loans instead of demanding immediate repayment. China has continued to roll over existing loans to Pakistan, providing Islamabad temporary relief from its foreign currency obligations without reducing its overall debt.With Pakistan struggling to repay its Chinese loans, what explains Beijing's willingness to not only continue providing financial support to Islamabad but also roll over existing loans?Sushant Sareen, senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation and an expert on Pakistan, attributed Beijing's continued support to the “strategic relationship” between the two countries.“It’s not just about an economic relationship between them. I think one of the reasons why the Chinese keep bailing Pakistan out and give them money is because of the strategic relationship that exists between them,” Sareen told The Times of India.Even CPEC, he added, was China’s plan to “prop up” Pakistan’s economy and make it more efficient and productive.Ultimately, the question is whether Pakistan can generate enough foreign exchange to service its growing debt, even with continued support from China.That Beijing is Islamabad’s largest creditor comes as little surprise. However, multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank also continue to play an important role in financing Pakistan.Since joining the IMF in 1950, Pakistan has received around two dozen bailout packages. Most recently, in October, the IMF agreed to release another $1.21 billion under its ongoing loan and sustainability programmes, subject to Executive Board approval.In a recent YouTube interview, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath was asked why the lender continues to bail out Pakistan despite concerns over its ability to repay its loans.Gopinath explained that the IMF’s role is to help countries facing economic crises and that it cannot simply walk away from them.She also emphasised that the IMF's decisions are taken by its member countries, including India. The decision to extend a loan, therefore, rests with the membership rather than the IMF's management.Sareen echoed this view.“Pakistan is a member of the IMF. It is the IMF’s job to bail out countries which are facing balance of payments problems,” he said.He, however, pointed out that political considerations could also influence the IMF's lending decisions.“India holds slightly over 2% vote share and that's not big enough to veto the loan. The Americans with 16% or 17% stake can actually do that, because with 15% you can veto any IMF loan. And clearly the Americans don't want to turn the screws on the Pakistanis. So, yes, to some extent it is a political decision to give money to Pakistan,” he argued.Sareen noted, however, that overall, the IMF largely operates within its economic mandate.Taken together, Islamabad's repeated reliance on the IMF underlines the extent to which its economy depends on external financial support.Pakistan's total external debt of around $135 billion does not mean the entire amount is due for repayment immediately. The debt has accumulated over several years, with repayments spread across different periods.The extent of Pakistan's reliance on fresh borrowing is evident from the figures. In FY26, it received $16.16 billion in external loans, while repaying around $14.44 billion in external public debt, including $11.20 billion in principal and $3.24 billion in interest, according to the ministry of economic affairs.The key question, therefore, is whether Islamabad can generate enough foreign exchange to meet these repayment obligations while managing its other economic needs.Sareen argued that the bigger challenge for Pakistan was not repaying its entire debt, but servicing it — having enough foreign exchange to meet repayment and interest obligations as they fall due.“Pakistans' problem is that they're not earning the kind of foreign exchange they require to service that debt. And the debt which they're taking on is increasing virtually every year. But for now, they're managing to tide it over. They managed to avoid default, but at a very high price,” he said.The challenge for Islamabad, therefore, is not just to keep securing loans, but to build an economy capable of meeting its repayment obligations without repeatedly relying on external support.Pakistan is often described as a country facing economic collapse and the risk of disintegration. Its continued dependence on external financing raises an important question: what would happen if lenders stopped extending fresh loans to Islamabad?The withdrawal of support from its lenders would not automatically push Pakistan into default or close to disintegration. Rather, it would face severe economic difficulties.Sareen warned that a default could trigger severe economic hardship, with Pakistan potentially spending three to four years trying to stabilise its economy and regain access to the international financial system. During this period, it could struggle to maintain imports and deal with foreign exchange shortages.But Pakistan continues to stay afloat — with support from international institutions, as well as countries whose financial assistance is shaped by strategic interests. Lending decisions also have a political dimension, with the interests and influence of powerful member countries playing a role.For now, creditors continue to extend financial support, even as concerns over Islamabad's ability to repay its debt persist.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015. China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. Pakistan spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt.

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. Article Title: Redrawing Pakistan: Ministers back 12-province plan but political, constitutional hurdles remain
Article Text:
Pakistan's 12-province proposal gains momentum as senior ministers back restructuring (Representative Image)

What the proposed 12-province map could look like

Political consensus remains the biggest hurdle

What the Constitution requires

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better governance. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. Speaking to Geo News, he said the country could consider creating 12 provinces, provided the boundaries were drawn on administrative rather than linguistic, ethnic or political grounds.“If there is a proposal for 12 provinces, then make it 12,” Asif said, adding that new units should not be created to serve “language, ethnicity or political interests”.Pakistan’s interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also revived the debate, suggesting a referendum to gauge public opinion on the contentious issue. His remarks have fuelled speculation that powerful quarters favour a broader restructuring of Pakistan's administrative map, with reports pointing to a possible constitutional exercise in 2027.No formal roadmap, however, has been announced. The proposed number of provinces, their boundaries and the process for creating them remain undecided.One proposal reported in Pakistani media envisages dividing Punjab into four provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan into three each, and Sindh into two. The plan could involve a nationwide referendum and a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, although neither has been confirmed as an approved government initiative.Supporters argue that the existing arrangement concentrates too much administrative and financial authority in provincial capitals leaving smaller cities and districts dependent on decisions taken far away.Asif has questioned whether federal funds transferred to provincial governments are reaching local institutions, arguing that decentralisation could bring decision-making and resources closer to communities. Advocates of the proposal say smaller provinces would make public services more accessible and help address uneven development.But the debate is not only about the size of administrative units. It also raises questions about whether creating more provinces would improve governance without stronger local governments and greater financial autonomy for districts.The proposal has exposed differences within the ruling coalition itself. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), led by Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, has firmly opposed any division of Sindh, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has yet to settle on a formal position.The two parties are coalition partners in the federal government. The PML-N has said it will announce its position if the matter comes before Parliament, despite some of its leaders backing the creation of smaller provinces.A cabinet member in the Shehbaz Sharif government said reaching agreement would be difficult without the support of the major political parties.The issue has also prompted speculation about a possible understanding between the government and the main opposition, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). PML-N leader and former federal minister Khawaja Saad Rafique has suggested that the establishment could offer relief to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in return for PTI's support for the proposed constitutional changes. There has been no confirmation of such a deal.Smaller parties have also entered the debate. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its demand for new administrative units in Sindh, while Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain has called for new provinces to be considered through consultation and in the national interest.The Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party has backed the proposal on administrative grounds, while Jamaat-i-Islami has argued that the creation of new provinces should go hand in hand with strengthening local governments.Even if political parties agree on the broad idea, redrawing provincial boundaries would require a demanding constitutional process.Under Article 239 of Pakistan's Constitution, an amendment requires the support of at least two-thirds of the total membership of both houses of Parliament. If it changes the limits of an existing province, it must also secure the backing of at least two-thirds of the total membership of that province's assembly.That gives provincial parties considerable leverage over any proposed division.A nationwide referendum is not an automatic constitutional requirement for creating provinces. Any such exercise would need its own legal and constitutional basis, and Parliament could not simply be bypassed in deciding the process or framing the questions put to voters.Following a meeting between Pakistan’s president Asif Ali Zardari and prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday, a senior government official told news agency PTI that the two leaders had agreed to adhere strictly to the constitutional provisions governing the creation of new provinces. They also agreed that any proposed referendum would require parliamentary approval.Former federal information minister Muhammad Ali Durrani has meanwhile launched a campaign for the restoration of Bahawalpur province and the creation of 11 other smaller administrative units.For now, the proposal remains a subject of political debate rather than an agreed government plan. Any move to redraw the map would require agreement on boundaries, resources, parliamentary representation and the future of provincial institutions — as well as the constitutional numbers to make it happen.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.

Article Title: 24 militants, four soldiers killed in separate clashes in Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, the Pakistan Army said on Saturday, PTI reported.The army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki.During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants, including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition, the military said.The army said the militants used armed quadcopters to target military vehicles on patrol. The attack killed Major Omer Minhas Nasir and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan.Separately, security forces conducted operations against militant hideouts in Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, 16 militants were killed in the engagements. Twelve were killed in an operation in Ali Khel, while two each were killed in Mir Ali and Datta Khel.Two soldiers, Havildar Asmat Ali and Naik Aftab Ali, were killed during the operations. The ISPR said both soldiers fought bravely and laid down their lives in the line of duty. It added that the operations had dealt a major blow to the militant network.Weapons and ammunition were recovered from the slain militants, who, according to the military, were involved in several terrorist activities, including the killing of civilians.Pakistan's federal government uses the term 'Fitna al-Khawarij' for militants belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

Article Title: Suicide car bombing at security checkpoint in Pakistan kills 5, injures 13

At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, a security official reported on Friday.The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district, along the N-25 national highway. The vehicle struck a Frontier Corps (FC) checkpoint, according to a security official quoted by PTI.The three militants killed in the attack included the bomber, while two civilians also died. However, Dawn, quoting Balochistan police, reported that at least 16 people were injured, including three members of the border forces.The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing, identifying the suicide attacker as Osama Shahwani and saying he had joined the organisation in 2022.A security official, however, said Shahwani's name had appeared in a missing-persons case in 2024. The official alleged that the incident pointed to the BLA's recruitment of young Baloch men and its attempts to mislead authorities about their whereabouts.The injured were shifted to nearby hospitals for treatment. Security agencies are investigating the attack and the circumstances surrounding the bomber's links to the insurgent group.
Article Summary: At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province. The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing. The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district.

Article Title: Pakistani teen mauled to death by tigress released from cage for TikTok video shoot
Article Text:
Pakistani teenager mauled to death after tigress freed for TikTok video in Lahore (Image source: X)

A 19-year-old Pakistani teenager was mauled to death by a tigress after it was let out of its cage for a TikTok video shoot.The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. He was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment on Wednesday, according to local reports.Police identified the arrested farm owner as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure. The animal subsequently lost control and attacked the worker, police said.The incident also triggered an investigation into an alleged attempt to conceal the circumstances of the death. Police said efforts were made to portray the attack as an incident involving a dog rather than a big cat. The animal has since been handed over to wildlife authorities.Authorities are examining whether the farm had the necessary permits to keep the animal and whether adequate safety measures were in place at the facility. A case has been registered and investigations into possible negligence are under way.In a statement, Lahore Police said that the pursuit of social media content could not come at the cost of human life. It said all aspects of the alleged negligence and the attempt to conceal the attack would be investigated.There has been some confusion in initial media reports over whether the animal was a tiger or a lion. Lahore Police's statement described it as a tigress.
Article Summary: The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure.

Article Title: Imran Khan-Asim Munir deal? Sisters' release from jail, hospital visit spark buzz in Pakistan
Article Text:
Release of Imran Khan's two sisters and his hospital visit fuel speculation of a possible political understanding with Pakistan's military establishment

PTI ready to make peace?

Nawaz Sharif , Benazir Bhutto precedent

Why a deal may not be straightforward

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Is Pakistan witnessing the first signs of a possible thaw between jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and the country's powerful military establishment? The release of two of his sisters and his recent hospital visit for eye treatment have come amid speculation that a political settlement involving Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has taken place.His sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were released on Thursday from Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail after the Punjab government withdrew their extended detention orders. The two had spent 53 days in custody after being detained ahead of a Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) protest march. Their sister Aleema Khan remains behind bars.The release came a day after Imran Khan was taken from Adiala Jail to Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for an eye examination and treatment. Doctors administered an injection for an issue affecting his right eye, besides treating his blood pressure. He was discharged in the early hours of Thursday and returned to prison.The developments have coincided with renewed speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, however, dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday, saying Khan and his family would receive whatever relief the courts granted them.The possibility of a rapprochement is not entirely new. In August, one of Imran Khan's closest aides, PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari, had told Reuters that the former prime minister would not confront the military if released."If Imran Khan was released tomorrow, hypothetically, he wouldn't do anything that would effectively damage the country," Bukhari had said, describing him as "magnanimous".He had also suggested that Munir could take the initiative to ease tensions, saying the army chief could extend a "healing hand" to the country."That doesn't mean you go loggerheads with the establishment, with the military leader," Bukhari said, adding that personal grievances could be set aside in the national interest.The remarks marked a notable shift in the PTI's public rhetoric after years of confrontation with the military establishment following Khan's ouster in a no-confidence vote in 2022.Bukhari, however, had mentioned that there were no talks between the PTI and the military. He also acknowledged that it was unclear whether Khan himself shared the willingness to reconcile being expressed by party leaders outside prison.The latest speculation has also been fuelled by opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai's claim in October that Khan could be facing pressure to accept an arrangement similar to those involving former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto.Sharif left Pakistan in 2000 after being ousted and imprisoned following the military coup led by General Pervez Musharraf. Bhutto spent years abroad in self-imposed exile after her government was dismissed in 1996.Achakzai alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz and Pakistan Peoples Party were part of a political arrangement that could pave the way for a similar outcome in Khan's case. However, he did not establish that any such agreement had been reached.An exile arrangement could potentially offer a way out of the prolonged confrontation, but there is no confirmation that Khan has agreed to leave Pakistan or that negotiations with Munir are under way.Imran Khan's relationship with the military establishment deteriorated after disagreements over key appointments and foreign policy. He has accused the military leadership, including Munir, of orchestrating his removal. The military denies interfering in politics.Despite being in prison since August 2023, Khan remains the central figure in Pakistan's political confrontation. His party continues to demand his release, access to family members and lawyers, and relief in the cases against him.The PTI's position also raises a crucial question: can its leadership outside prison negotiate or signal a compromise without Khan's explicit approval? Bukhari's August remarks came with the caveat that the former prime minister's own thinking might be different.For now, the signals remain contradictory. Two members of Khan's family have been released, he has received medical treatment, and a senior PTI aide has previously spoken of reconciliation. But the government has denied any political bargain, and there is no evidence of direct negotiations with Munir.Whether the latest developments represent isolated legal and medical decisions or the beginning of a fresh political opening remains the question.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's two sisters were released from jail on Thursday after 53 days in custody. He was also taken to a hospital for an eye examination and treatment. The developments have fuelled speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday.

Article Title: Explained: 'Poverty, prejudice and profit', how Dhaka was repackaged as New Delhi
Article Text:
Chinese citizens making live videos from Dhaka

Chinese nationals films the streets of Uttara as part of the livestreaming activity reported in the area. PC credit: Prothom Alo

‘This is New Delhi’: What the livestreams showed

Bangladesh police stepped up surveillance in Uttara after reports about Chinese nationals filming in the neighbourhood. Credit: Bangla Vision

A trail that predates the controversy

When disgust becomes currency: How viral outrage shapes perceptions of India

A Chinese national films in Tekpara, adjacent to Uttara's Sector 12. Credit: Prothom Alo

The commercial angle and unanswered questions

How Dhaka was presented as New Delhi​

India objects; Bangladesh steps up surveillance

MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said efforts to present a distorted picture of a country were unfortunate.

The China contrast: Censorship and ‘positive energy’

Residents raise concerns about repeated filming in residential areas.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A question of accountability

A narrow lane in Dhaka. Modest homes, roadside tea stalls, a canal and residents going about their daily lives. A woman points her camera at the surroundings and tells her online audience: “This is New Delhi. ”The camera keeps moving. Tin-roofed houses are described as dirty and unhygienic. A neighbourhood in Bangladesh is presented as India's capital, while another livestreamer filming people drinking tea makes a grotesque claim about what is in their cups.These were not scenes from Delhi. They were filmed in Uttara and Tekpara, low-income neighbourhoods of Dhaka, by Chinese nationals.For months, the cameras reportedly kept returning to the same streets, homes and markets. Residents said they were filmed for hours, sometimes inside their own homes, without fully knowing where the footage was going or how their lives were being portrayed.Then, around November 7, the cameras began disappearing.The reports have since triggered an official response from New Delhi and increased surveillance by Bangladeshi law enforcement. But the most important questions remain unanswered: Who were these livestreamers working for? Why were Dhaka neighbourhoods being presented as Delhi? And was this a commercial content operation, an organised attempt to discredit India, or something more complicated?In its November 6 investigation, Bangladesh's Prothom Alo reported that Chinese nationals had been filming in Uttara's Sector 12 and the adjoining Tekpara area for months, often from morning until night.They were seen carrying two mobile phones, using one to livestream while apparently referring to material on the other.The newspaper said local residents estimated that more than 150 Chinese nationals were involved, although it acknowledged that no accurate count was available. Its reporters visited the neighbourhood on October 27 and November 3 and attempted to speak to 17 Chinese nationals. Most declined to answer questions.One livestreamer, identified as Mianmian and said to be from China's Sichuan province, was filmed beside a canal in Sector 12 on November 1. While showing the surrounding neighbourhood, she told viewers: “This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses. This place is quite underdeveloped, dirty and unhygienic, and the law-and-order situation is poor.”Another streamer, identified as Wang Wei, was reportedly filming at tea stalls in Tekpara when he told viewers: “Look, they are drinking tea. Do you know what kind of tea this is? This is cow urine tea. They drink cow urine tea.”Prothom Alo said it translated portions of the Chinese-language broadcasts using Google Translate and had the translations checked by four Bangladeshis familiar with Chinese.The issue extended beyond the misrepresentation of locations. Residents complained that cameras were repeatedly pointed at their homes and private lives, sometimes without permission.“Sometimes they enter our homes and start filming. We are not always properly dressed inside our houses. Imagine how it feels when someone suddenly walks into your home and starts recording,” resident Rozina Khatun told the Bangladeshi media outlet.Another resident, Papia Begum, said some streamers even entered bathrooms while filming. She said objections often led them to apologise and leave, but they returned later.The November revelations were not the first reports of Chinese nationals filming in the area. A May 23 investigation reported that Chinese vloggers had been filming in Tekpara for hours at a time, sometimes using iPhones fitted with cooling fans.Videos from the neighbourhoods have also appeared on Chinese platforms such as Bilibili and Youku. Several reportedly carry titles using disparaging terms such as “poor”, “dirty” and “slum”, while focusing on low-income residents and their living conditions.In May, Bangladeshi media outlets reported on videos in which creators appeared to portray themselves as benefactors helping impoverished residents. One resident alleged that a vlogger had grabbed a young Bangladeshi man's collar in a video, apparently to “discipline” him.The repeated circulation of videos portraying India through poverty, dirt and deprivation can also be understood through the idea of an epistemic project — the process through which selected images, labels and narratives shape how audiences understand a country. When viewers repeatedly encounter footage described as “dirty”, “backward” or “unliveable”, these portrayals can gradually become familiar reference points, influencing perceptions beyond the individual videos.Disgust, shock and anger can also make viewers stop scrolling, react to content and share it. Repeated exposure to such selective imagery can also reinforce stereotypes about an entire country.A March 2026 study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, involving five experiments and 1,051 participants, found that people tended to overestimate the emotional intensity of reactions in their social-media feeds. Such perceptions were associated with a greater willingness to share content.The commercial incentive is clear. JNU professor Srikanth Kondapalli told ANI that some Chinese creators seek online recognition and validation. “They want to establish a higher profile on Weibo, WeChat and other social networking platforms. Their social standing and prestige increase with the number of subscribers, likes and validation they receive for their videos,” he said.There is also a commercial explanation offered by at least one person involved. When Prothom Alo approached a Chinese national identified as Fangyou, a local guide helped translate the questions. Fangyou said the livestreams on WeChat were part of product-promotion activities. He declined to explain why the group had selected that particular neighbourhood or why the broadcasts continued for such long hours.Ritu Akhter, a Bangladeshi woman who said she had worked as a guide for the Chinese nationals for several months, told the newspaper she earned between 700 and 800 taka a day. She said other local women were also doing similar work.Some shopkeepers were reportedly paid around 500 taka to allow filming in their pharmacies, where Indian consumer products such as shampoo, soap and Kesh King hair oil were used as backdrops for promotional livestreams.These accounts point to a possible commercial component, but leave key questions unanswered: which products were being promoted, who owned the accounts, who paid the creators and local facilitators, and why some broadcasts allegedly labelled Dhaka as Delhi. No publicly established evidence has identified a commissioning organisation or a funding trail.India's ministry of external affairs raised the matter on November 10. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “We have seen media reports in this regard. Such efforts to present a distorted picture of any country are unfortunate.”Referring to reports of foreign elements being used to portray Dhaka as Delhi, he added: “Peddling of false narratives only undermines the credibility of those who are undertaking such actions and those who are behind them. And I would urge that authorities concerned must take action against such a report.”Bangladeshi authorities subsequently stepped up monitoring. Mohammad Khalid Mansur, officer-in-charge of Uttara West Police Station, told Prothom Alo that the activities of the Chinese nationals had declined after law enforcement intervention. Police and intelligence personnel were monitoring their movements, he said.According to the newspaper, some Chinese nationals were asked to produce their passports and visas and explain why they were undertaking the filming while visiting on tourist visas. They were also told to leave after their permitted stay expired.By November 11, the newspaper's correspondent had not seen Chinese nationals livestreaming in the areas visited. Resident Imam ul Islam, a rickshaw puller, said: “They would make videos here day and night. They filmed us and the passengers too. I haven't seen them for some time.”The controversy also invites scrutiny of the information environment in which the footage was reportedly being circulated. China's domestic internet is not an unrestricted marketplace of images and opinions. Its authorities have established rules that direct platforms to regulate content and promote officially approved narratives.In September 2025, China's Cyberspace Administration (CAC) launched a campaign targeting posts it accused of exaggerating personal hardships, spreading pessimism and promoting “world-weariness”. Major platforms, including Weibo, Kuaishou and Xiaohongshu, were directed to remove such content. Critics viewed the measures as an attempt to curb narratives that could undermine the government's portrayal of economic progress.Freedom House's Freedom on the Net 2024 report also documented the removal of online content depicting poverty and economic hardship, including the censorship of the film Return to Dust and its title on Sina Weibo.This provides context for examining how narratives about poverty are regulated within China while some influencers have circulated disparaging portrayals of India. However, it does not establish that the Dhaka vloggers were acting on government instructions or had official backing.This record provides context for examining the contrast between the image of China promoted through its regulated digital environment and the freedom with which some creators appear to have circulated disparaging portrayals of another country. It does not, however, establish that the vloggers in Dhaka were acting under state instructions, or that Chinese authorities approved their broadcasts.For Bangladesh, the immediate questions concern the rights of residents, the conduct of foreign visitors and whether filming or commercial activity breached visa conditions.For India, the issue is the circulation of content that allegedly attributes another country's locations and living conditions to its capital. For China, questions remain about the platforms carrying the broadcasts and whether their location claims and commentary were subject to any scrutiny.
Article Summary: Chinese nationals have been filming in Dhaka's Uttara and Tekpara neighbourhoods for months. Residents say they were filmed for hours, sometimes inside their own homes. One livestreamer told viewers: “This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses’

Article Title: At least 30 houses of Awami members set on fire in Bangladesh
Article Text:
Over 50 houses and several shops belonging to Awami League leaders and activists were set ablaze

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

DHAKA: Following the killing of two BNP leaders on Wednesday, at least 20 to 30 houses belonging to leaders and activists of the Awami League (AL) were set on fire in attacks allegedly carried out by BNP activists in Kalia upazila of Narail district.Several other houses and shops were also reportedly vandalised and looted during the attacks in Bendar Char village from Friday afternoon until midnight. Narail superintendent of police Mohammad Al Mamun Sikder told reporters on Saturday that relatives and supporters of the two slain BNP leaders had vandalised three to four houses in the village.District police rejected social media reports that Hindu families' homes and businesses had been attacked, vandalised or looted. On Nov 18, leaders and activists of the now-banned Awami League had attacked a BNP procession. As a result, two individuals were killed: Shahin Sheikh (45), general secretary of Kalia Municipal Krishak Dal and Sohel Molla (40), general secretary of JASAS-Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Samajik Sanskritik Sangstha, Kalia Upazila. Later, police arrested Dipsha Biswas (31) and Rakib Biswas (21), residents of Bendar Char in Narail.Rescue personnel who visited the scene found 20 to 30 houses on fire, although the extent of damage could be higher. The BNP, however, denied the allegations.
Article Summary: At least 20 to 30 houses belonging to leaders and activists of the Awami League (AL) were set on fire in attacks allegedly carried out by BNP activists in Kalia upazila of Narail district. Several other houses and shops were also reportedly vandalised and looted during the attacks in Bendar Char village.

Article Title: 'Place national interest first': Opposition tells Nepal PM ahead of first India visit
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nepal's opposition Nepali Congress on Saturday urged Prime Minister Balendra Shah to prioritise national interest during his upcoming visit to New Delhi.Shah is set to embark on a two-day visit to India on Sunday, leading a 34-member delegation.Nepali Congress senior vice president Bishwa Prakash Sharma, in a statement, said the visit should serve Nepal's interests while further strengthening ties between the two countries.According to news agency PTI, the party said it had held internal discussions with subject-matter experts to offer the government constructive suggestions on areas of bilateral cooperation.The discussions covered climate change, air connectivity, tourism, trade, energy, sports, entrepreneurship, border management, concerns of people living in border areas, and challenges faced by Nepali workers in India, the statement said."Nepal-India relations should be grounded in mutual respect, sovereign equality, and national interest," the party said.As Shah is set to visit India representing Nepal, the Nepali Congress said broad consultations and a shared understanding on matters of national interest would strengthen the country's standing on the international forum.The party said it remained committed to protecting Nepal's interests and strengthening ties with its friendly neighbour India.The visit should focus on implementing commitments made in the past, resolving outstanding issues and laying the groundwork for long-term cooperation based on mutual benefit, it said.This will be Shah's first bilateral visit to any country since he assumed office on March 27. He travelled to the United States in September to attend the United Nations General Assembly.During the visit, Shah will call on President Droupadi Murmu and hold delegation-level talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar will also pay a courtesy call on Shah, Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told media persons at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Friday.Shah had received an invitation from Modi to visit India when the government led by the Rastriya Swatantra Party leader was formed in March, around six months after the youth-led Gen Z protests toppled the K P Sharma Oli government in September last year.
Article Summary: Nepal's opposition Nepali Congress urges Prime Minister Balendra Shah to prioritise national interest during his upcoming visit to New Delhi. Shah is set to embark on a two-day visit to India on Sunday, leading a 34-member delegation.

Article Title: Bangladesh wage protests: Clashes erupt between garment workers and police, dozens of factories shut
Article Text:
To maintain control, the police deployed tear gas to break up the protest after production was halted. (Pic Credit: AP)

Tensions escalated in Bangladesh's Ashulia on Saturday as garment workers demanding a hike in minimum wages clashed with security forces. Police fired tear gas to disperse the protesters and bring the situation under control, The Daily Star reported.According to the news agency ANI, the confrontation took place around 11 am in the Kathgara area along the Zirabo-Bismail road. Workers from several garment factories had stopped production and joined the protest, according to the report.Eyewitnesses told The daily star that workers at multiple factories in Kathgara first entered their workplaces before stopping work. They later organised a rally and attempted to block the road around 10:45 am after factory management announced holidays.Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police at industrial police-1 in Ashulia, said in a text message around noon that the situation had returned to normal."Some unruly workers were trying to create instability at the garment factories that remained operational in the Kathgara area. Industrial police and other forces intervened to keep the situation under control," Bhuiyan said.Earlier on Saturday, at least 50 factories in the Savar-Ashulia industrial belt announced holidays following work stoppages.However, most factories in the area had started operations as usual in the morning, industrial police told the newspaper.The latest clashes come amid continuing protests by garment workers across Bangladesh over demands for higher wages and better working conditions.On Tuesday, garment workers staged demonstrations in Mirpur, Dhaka, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be increased to 30,000 taka. The protests came as labour unrest spread across the country's textile industry, forcing several factories to suspend operations.Protesters also attempted to block roads but were stopped by police, who intervened to prevent traffic disruptions and maintain law and order.Garment workers in several parts of Bangladesh have been staging strikes to demand better pay, with demonstrations leading to factory closures in multiple industrial areas, DW reported.Separately, a group of workers gathered at Padmar Mor in the Hemayetpur area of Savar around 3 pm on Monday, briefly disrupting the area. Police asked them to disperse peacefully, following which they cleared the road without further incident, Dhaka Tribune reported.Meanwhile, around 40 factories remained closed in the Savar and Ashulia industrial zones on Monday, according to industrial police.Of these, 27 factories were shut under section 13(1) of the Bangladesh labour act, while nine were declared closed indefinitely. The remaining factories observed general holidays.Bhuiyan said workers at one factory refused to resume work after the lunch break and continued sitting inside the premises, prompting management to declare a holiday. Employees at two other factories also stopped work and staged sit-in protests inside their workplaces.However, workers at other factories across the industrial areas continued their operations peacefully, he added.
Article Summary: Police fired tear gas to disperse the protesters and bring the situation under control. The confrontation took place around 11 am in the Kathgara area along the Zirabo-Bismail road. Workers from several garment factories had stopped production and joined the protest.

Article Title: ‘Justice at last’: Rohingya refugees welcome UN court action against Myanmar
Article Text:
The court held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya minority

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar, a landmark ruling by UN court recognising Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown as genocide has brought renewed hope for justice and a safe return home. Refugees gathered around a large screen at the camp on Thursday to follow the verdict, which many described as a “small victory”.The court held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya minority, marking the first time it has ruled that a state committed the crime. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees, pay reparations and prosecute those suspected of involvement in the atrocities.However, refugees told The Washington Post that the ruling was only the beginning of their fight. “Justice has started,” said Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader, adding that they still had “a long way to go”.The judgment comes nearly nine years after Myanmar’s military launched a clearance operation in Rakhine state in August 2017, following an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The crackdown was accompanied by allegations of mass killings, sexual violence and the burning of thousands of homes.The ICJ said evidence showed Myanmar's forces killed around 10,000 Rohingya.Despite the legally binding nature of the verdict, its implementation remains uncertain as the court has no independent enforcement mechanism. Myanmar's government on Friday dismissed the ruling as “unfair”.Around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees currently live in Bangladesh, most in overcrowded camps in Cox’s Bazar, facing poor sanitation, disease, fire hazards and restrictions on employment. Bangladesh has repeatedly called on the international community to help facilitate their return to Myanmar.
Article Summary: The court held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya minority. It is the first time it has ruled that a state committed the crime. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees, pay reparations and prosecute those suspected of involvement in the atrocities.

Article Title: Bangladesh minister house targeted in petrol bomb attack

Article Title: Indian Team leaves for Bangladesh for talks on Ganga water
Article Text: NEW DELHI: A four-member team from India headed to Bangladesh Friday to attend a meeting of the joint committee constituted under Ganga Water Treaty between the two countries to monitor the sharing of the river's waters. The meeting is scheduled for Nov 21-23.The visit comes weeks before the 30-year-old treaty is due to lapse on Dec 12, even as the team, led by head of India's Joint Rivers Commission Sharad Chandra, visiting Dhaka doesn't have the mandate to discuss the agreement's extension beyond its existing term.Sources hinted that it is for the political leadership of both nations to take a call on its renewal or interim extension and its terms, whatever the case may be. Bangladesh has said instead of renewing the existing one, it wants to negotiate a new treaty with India, including a clause guaranteeing that its required share of water during the dry season is protected.
Article Summary: A four-member team from India headed to Bangladesh Friday to attend a meeting of the joint committee constituted under Ganga Water Treaty. The visit comes weeks before the 30-year-old treaty is due to lapse on Dec 12. Bangladesh has said instead of renewing the existing one, it wants to negotiate a new treaty with India.

Article Title: ‘ICJ ruling made world finally record our pain & loss,’ say Rohingya refugees at Bangladesh camp
Article Text:

After the landmark judgment by International Court of Justice (ICJ), terming the killings of Rohingyas by Myanmar junta forces as “genocide”, displaced community members living in the world’s largest refugee settlement of Kutupalong camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, hailed the verdict as a “global acknowledgement of their unparalleled suffering, pain and loss”.Speaking toover phone on Friday, Ak Mohammed Sadek, 27, a Rohingya who arrived at the Cox’s Bazar camp with his mother and six siblings in 2017, said that everyone at the settlement were nervously following the news on their radios.“We’ve suffered for a decade… The world has now finally recorded our immense pain. This strengthens our hope of returning home one day -- with dignity and honour,” said Sadek, who claimed to have witnessed his father shot dead and an aunt burnt alive after rape in 2017. He was a Class 10 student at that time and lost at least nine members of his family.Sadek added that he had to run for his life from Dhumsay Para village in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.“After my father, I lost my mother to a serious ailment at the camp. She was heartbroken after seeing what she shouldn’t have,” the 27-year-old said.Twenty-six-year-old Sanaullah Omar fled his village with his parents and two siblings that same year to be at the refugee camp.“The UN top court’s judgment on Thursday has given us the will to live and fight again,” he said, adding that “the violence we suffered in 2017 haunts me and others all the time. It flashes before my eyes.”Omar’s father was a village head who saw his dwellings burnt down. “We walked on empty stomachs through dense forests and travelled on a boat for around five days to reach Cox’s Bazar,” he added. After completing his classes 9 and 10 at the refugee camp school, Omar now works as a teacher at an UNICEF-run school within the settlement.Laila Begam’s fate and destiny seemed to be similar to those of Sadek and Omar, both much younger than her. Like them, she escaped death with her family of 10 that year.“Today is an emotional day for me. Though I don’t understand much of the court ruling, I only know that they (ICJ) have told the world that a crime like that should not go unpunished. Since the ruling, I’ve been praying for the departed souls...,” said Begam, with several pauses as her voice shook with emotion.She told: “I’m 65. But, I still hope I’ll see my home in Myanmar some day.”According to data on the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees’ website, the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement hosts around 11.7 lakh Rohingya refugees who fled violence in Myanmar.Meanwhile, Bangladesh minister of foreign affairs, Khalilur Rahman, who holds the position of president of 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), visited the settlement at Cox’s Bazar on Friday.Terming the ICJ verdict as “final and unequivocal”, he said: “While the judgment can’t bring back the dead or heal everyone, the truth is, justice begins now. After considering all the evidence and hearing Myanmar’s arguments, ICJ made it clear that what was done to the Rohingyas in 2017 was a genocide.”Myanmar govt spokesperson, Khaing Khaing Soe, meanwhile said in capital Naypyidaw that his country was “unjustly accused”. He added: “This decision is not unanimous; it is not fair.”ICJ said on Thursday that “mass executions of men and boys, widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burning or razing of hundreds of villages” were carried out during the so-called clearance operations in Myanmar.
